# title: HIS-201 Ch. 13 — 5 Q&A

What characterized the South under "King Cotton"?
column2: Cotton fueled the southern economy, drove slaves and settlers west and south, and by 1860 made the United States the producer of three-fourths of the world's cotton, yet the region stayed overwhelmingly rural, lagging in manufacturing, cities, and schools.

column1: How did the Upper South and the Deep South differ?
column2: The Upper South, with exhausted soils, shifted toward wheat and corn, needed less slave labor, and sold about 2 million people to the Lower South, while the Deep South's cotton, rice, and sugar plantations became the main destination of that trade and, in South Carolina and Mississippi, had Black majorities.

column1: What was the relationship between the planter class and yeoman farmers?
column2: Planters were a tiny elite—only about 1 in 30 white southerners—while yeomen, more than half of whites, were a landowning middle class hurt socially and economically by slavery; even so, yeomen supported the institution out of racism and fear of emancipation and often claimed they were "as good as" planters.

column1: What were the living conditions of enslaved African Americans?
column2: Slaves lived in cramped, poorly built, leaky and drafty cabins with only crude furniture, received inadequate clothing and shelter, and got less than a dollar a year in medical care, so a deficient diet and hard labor produced a lower life expectancy than among whites.

column1: What was a typical slave diet?
column2: The weekly ration was about a peck of cornmeal, 3 or 4 pounds of bacon or salt pork, and molasses, almost 5,400 calories but a monotonous corn-and-pork fare lacking several essential nutrients and associated with pellagra and beriberi, which slaves often supplemented from gardens, hunting, or theft.

column1: What were slaves' work and free-time routines?
column2: Toil began just before sunrise and lasted until dusk, reaching 15 to 16 hours a day at cultivation and harvest, with work uncommon on Sundays and often only a half day on Saturdays, and holidays sometimes brought banquets even as the everyday routine remained taxing.

column1: What role did religion play in slave life?
column2: Many slaves joined southern Methodist and Baptist churches, where they made up more than a quarter of the members, but most also sought a Christianity of their own in hush harbors, using spirituals such as "Steal Away to Jesus" to express dignity and a hidden longing for freedom.

column1: How did enslaved people resist their owners?
column2: Most resistance was day-to-day: running away (especially hard except from the border states), mishandling animals, breaking tools, working carelessly, feigning illness, hiding rocks in the cotton, and, most commonly, theft, plus an "impenetrable mask" that hid true feelings from whites.

column1: What significant organized resistance to slavery occurred in the South?
column2: Well-organized uprisings were rare in the United States compared with Latin America; Gabriel Prosser's 1800 plot and Denmark Vesey's 1822 conspiracy were betrayed, and the most famous revolt was Nat Turner's in 1831, which killed 57 whites before it was crushed.

column1: How did the lives of free southern Blacks compare with those of slaves?
column2: Free Blacks, about 7 percent of southern African Americans, were not slaves and were more urban and more literate, and some even owned family members, but they occupied an uncertain place beneath even poorer whites, with few economic opportunities and tightening legal restrictions.

column1: What restrictions did free Black southerners face after Nat Turner's Rebellion?
column2: After 1831 they were forbidden to enter a different state, had to carry freedom papers, could not assemble as they wished, faced a curfew, often had to post a bond and be licensed to work, and could not vote, hold office, or testify in court against white people.

column1: What was the significance of the Virginia Debate of 1832?
column2: In the aftermath of Nat Turner's revolt, the legislature debated slavery from January 16 to 25 and then refused to act, 73 to 58, making this the last significant attempt of white southerners to challenge the peculiar institution before the Civil War.

column1: How did the gang system differ from the task system?
column2: Under the gang system, used especially in cotton districts, an overseer or driver supervised groups of about 20 to 25 adults for long, closely watched hours; under the task system, most common in rice fields, each slave had a daily assignment and was finished when it was done.

column1: What was paternalism, and how did it compare with reality?
column2: Defenders of slavery stressed the planter's role as a protective father, but the book says this was more the ideal than the reality, and that slavery everywhere rested on violence, racism, and exploitation, with the whip the most common punishment.

column1: How did Tidewater plantation districts differ from the cotton frontier?
column2: Tidewater society along the Chesapeake and South Carolina coast was older and more refined, with English-country-gentleman ideals and Greek Revival mansions, while the cotton frontier was rawer, full of self-made men, unpretentious homes, and a boom mentality of selling cotton to buy more slaves.

column1: Why did the South lag in cities and manufacturing?
column2: Single-crop agriculture and slavery kept the region rural, so 84 percent of its labor force still farmed in 1860 and it produced only 9 percent of the nation's manufactures; with so little industry, few cities developed, and the lack of a dense domestic market further slowed growth.

column1: Why did most nonslaveowning whites still support slavery?
column2: Yeomen were hurt socially and economically by the institution, and poor whites resented planters, but both groups disliked Black people even more intensely, feared emancipation, and shared a belief in white equality and opportunity that tied them to the slave regime.

column1: What environmental problems did southern agriculture create?
column2: Single-crop farming rapidly wore out the soil, tobacco and corn were especially exhausting, and when Upper South farmers shifted to wheat and plowed their fields instead of using a hoe, the change intensified soil erosion.

column1: What arguments did white southerners use to defend slavery?
column2: Proslavery writers offered religious and racial justifications, claimed that slaves lived better than factory workers, and, as one editor put it, sought to satisfy white southerners "that slavery is of itself right—that it is not a sin against God—that it is not an evil, moral or political."

column1: If the slave population increased naturally, why was life expectancy still lower?
column2: The United States was the only slave society in the Americas where the slave population increased naturally, even at about the same rate as the white population, but a deficient diet, inadequate clothing and shelter, long hours of hard toil, and poor medical care still produced a lower life expectancy.

column1: How did slavery become more central to southern identity after 1831?
column2: As the economy grew more dependent on slave-produced staples, and after The Liberator and Turner's revolt, white southerners rallied to defend the institution, so that outside the border states few after 1840 would admit even in private that slavery was wrong.

column1: Was the Old South only a land of elegant planters and obedient slaves?
column2: No: the book opens with many "real Souths"—rice grandees, cotton men, industrial slaves, runaways, and yeomen—and stresses that most slaveowners owned only a few slaves, while the majority of southern whites were nonslaveowning yeoman farmers.
